vignette: Arjun stands in the sterile hallway, eight years ago, watching the double doors swing shut on his son's room. He is fifty, but his hands remember the weight of wire cutters, the steady rhythm of a detonator's countdown. Now, the only rhythm that matters is the flatline approaching the monitor. The pediatrician speaks in low, measured tones. Arjun nods, swallows the bile rising in his throat, and waits. When the beep returns, steady and strong, he exhales. He does not cry. He walks out into the Lahore summer heat, his chest hollowed out by a fear he cannot name, carrying a silence that will outlast his career. The silence hardens into routine. For months, Arjun sleeps on the sofa, waking when the refrigerator hums or a branch scrapes the window. He tells himself he is merely tired, merely adjusting. But his body has learned a new language. At the precinct, he reviews defusal protocols with mechanical precision, yet his fingers tremble when he reaches for his coffee. He begins checking the stove seven times. He avoids hospitals, then clinics, then doctors' offices, until he stops going to the pharmacy for his wife's asthma inhalers. He tells Meera he is fine. He tells himself the same thing. He buys a new wire cutter. He maps escape routes in every restaurant. He learns to sit perfectly still while his mind rehearses flatlines, his pulse drumming against his collarbone like a faulty timer. He stops answering calls after six. He tells Meera his phone is broken. He listens to the silence instead. Now, at fifty-eight, the world feels like a room full of unexploded charges. He works in the evidence bay, cataloging seized devices, his colleagues respecting his quiet focus. They bring him chai, joke about his meticulous notes. He smiles, adjusts his cotton gloves, and handles each item with deliberate care. But inside, he is listening. He times how long it takes for the radio to crackle. He notes the weight of the paper stack. He watches the door. Control used to be his compass. Now, control feels like a mirror reflecting a man who no longer recognizes his own reflection. He eats alone. He stops attending the Friday prayers. He tells Meera he is just tired, then apologizes for his tone. He watches her shoulders tighten. He wants to reach for her hand. His fingers remain still, anchored by a habit of self-isolation he cannot quite explain. He tells himself he is protecting her from his weight. Yesterday, he walked past a community center. A child's soccer ball bounced against the pavement, a sound like a dropped wrench. Arjun stopped. His breath caught. His jaw locked. He stood on the sidewalk, waiting for the panic to pass, watching a man tie his shoelaces, watching a dog shake its coat, watching rain begin to fall. He told himself he was fine. He told himself he had handled worse. But the truth settles in his posture, heavy and unyielding: he is still in that hallway. He is still watching the monitor. He is still waiting for the beep that proves his boy is safe. It happens, every day. The waiting never stops.
